story: Mars's tiny, potato-shaped moon Phobos bears a colossal battle scar: Stickney crater. Measuring nine kilometers across on a moon only twenty-seven kilometers long, Stickney dominates nearly half of Phobos's width. The impact that carved it was so violent that it came within inches of shattering the entire moon into rubble. Phobos only survived because of its bizarre, highly porous interior, which absorbed the cataclysmic shock like a cosmic sponge. Today, landslides streak Stickney's walls under a gravitational pull less than one-thousandth of Earth's, while mysterious grooves wrap around the moon's surface. Scientists suspect these trenches might be tracks left by giant boulders ejected from Stickney rolling completely around the moon, or stretch marks from Mars tearing it apart. Though Phobos survived an impact that should have obliterated it, its days are numbered: Martian tidal forces are pulling it inward, doomed to rip it apart within fifty million years.
angle: The collision that created Stickney crater was violent enough to blast Phobos into pieces, but the moon survived because its interior was so porous it absorbed the cataclysm like a sponge.
disputed: The origin of the grooves on Phobos: hypotheses attribute them to rolling impact boulders, tidal stretch marks from Mars, or Martian impact ejecta; a script should attribute these as competing scientific hypotheses.
The precise diameter of Stickney crater: sources cite 9 km, 'over 9 km', or '6-mile-wide (10 km)'; a script should state it is approximately 9 kilometers across.

The ultimate fate of Phobos: sources mention either structural breakup into a ring in 30 to 50 million years or crashing into Mars in 50 million years; a script should state it will be pulled apart or destroyed within 30 to 50 million years.
